items.stem: In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", how does attention decide that "it" refers to "animal"?

options.text: It scores every word on how well it matches what "it" asks for, and animal scores highest.
options.feedback: The score is a similarity between positions. Tired asks for something that can be tired, and animal matches.

options.text: A grammar rule says a pronoun refers to the subject of the sentence.
options.feedback: The model uses no grammar rule. The result changes when the last word changes.

options.text: It picks the nearest noun, because words close together are usually related.
options.feedback: Street is nearer to "it" than animal is, and the model still picks animal.

options.text: It picks the noun that was read first, because earlier words count for more.
options.feedback: The order of reading plays no part. Every word is available at once.

items.stem: You change the last word of the sentence from "tired" to "wide". What happens to what "it" looks at?

options.text: It shifts toward "street", because wide describes a street.
options.feedback: "It" builds its question from the words around it. Wide asks for something with width, and street matches.

options.text: It stays on "animal", because the nouns in the sentence have not changed.
options.feedback: The question that "it" asks depends on the last word, so the weights change.

options.text: It spreads evenly across all the words in the sentence.
options.feedback: The weights stay concentrated on the best match.

options.text: It looks only at the last word, because that word changed.
options.feedback: The last word gets some weight, and the strongest weight goes to street.

items.stem: A prompt grows from 4,000 tokens to 8,000 tokens. Roughly how does the attention work change?

options.feedback: Every token is compared with every other token, so the work grows with the square of the length.

options.text: It doubles, in line with the length.
options.feedback: Doubling would be true if each token were compared with a fixed number of others. Here each token is compared with all the others.

options.text: It stays the same, whatever the length.

options.feedback: Doubling the length multiplies the work by four.

items.stem: Why did attention remove the problem of the single note in recurrent networks?

options.text: Every word stays available, so any word can look at any other directly.
options.feedback: Nothing is summarized away. Word 1 and word 5,000 are one step apart.

options.text: The note was made much larger, so it holds the whole sentence.
options.feedback: A transformer has no note. The words themselves are kept.

options.text: The model skips most words and reads only the important ones.
options.feedback: All words are kept and compared.

options.text: Words are read in a random order, which avoids the fading.
options.feedback: The order is still part of the input. A word's reach no longer depends on reading order.
